# Developing an applied extreme heat vulnerability index utilizing socioeconomic and environmental data

## Abstract

Extreme heat is a leading cause of weather-related fatalities worldwide. Emphasis is currently being placed on the development of spatially specific vulnerability models, which are useful for decision support during extreme heat events (EHE). Research results concerning such spatially-explicit models lead efforts in preparation and mitigation of heat-related vulnerability and potential adaptation. The presented research analyzes the 1995 Chicago EHE in the context of a socio-environmental hazards approach, and fosters the development of an extreme heat vulnerability index (EHVI). The EHVI is a fused dataset consisting of census data and remotely sensed variables, which are examined in relation to geocoded mortality data. The presented analysis combines 25 well-known indicators of extreme heat-health risk into an applied index utilizing a principal components analysis. The developed EHVI presented a trend of higher rates of death in the highest risk zones to lower rates in lower zones of risk. The model explains nearly 80% of the total variance in the heat-health vulnerability variables utilized. This index could be utilized by city officials to assist in the mitigation of extreme heat events and is a further evolution of previously developed efforts. Our findings indicate extreme heat vulnerability models should likely be developed on a local level for a specific location, taking into account local variations in social and environmental vulnerability.

## Introduction

Extreme heat is a leading cause of weather-related mortality in the United States (Patz et al., 2000). The summer of 2011 recorded the hottest temperatures in North America for 75 years, breaking many of the previously held modern record temperatures. One summer of excessive temperatures alone does not constitute overall concern; but when it is placed into context with recent climate models, which predict more intense and prolonged heat waves, it becomes a cause for greater concern. Coupling this with the fact that most communities in North America are poorly equipped to deal with excesses in temperature, the need for understanding the hazardous nature of extreme heat becomes paramount (Jackson & Shields, 2008).

Highlighting groups or populations that are especially susceptible (or vulnerable) to the effects of extreme heat is centrally important to communities as they develop contingency plans for a changing climate. Vulnerability, whether to extreme heat or something else, is a complex concept that is multidimensional in scope. It is typically defined as the inability, of a specific group or population, to appropriately respond or adapt to a specific harmful stressor (Andrew, Mitnitski, & Rockwood, 2008; Bankoff, 2001; Blaikie, Cannon, Davis, & Wisner, 1994). Vulnerability is oftentimes confused with risk, which is defined as the potential for a harmful or disadvantageous event. Since vulnerability is a multidimensional concept, its relationship to risk from natural hazards can be examined from multiple perspectives. Historically, it has been common to place explicit emphasis on the natural phenomena that are responsible for risk (Wisner, 2004). A natural output of this approach might specify the location where a hazard is likely to occur and draw a conclusion that persons in close proximity to the effected area are most “at-risk”; employing a hazard-first focus with disregard for underlying social aspects. An alternate approach is to examine the “social vulnerability” of an existing population (Bankoff, 2003; Cutter, Boruff, & Shirley, 2003; Cutter & Finch, 2008). Typically evidenced by socioeconomic status, social vulnerability implies that a population is at-risk due to social characteristics intrinsic and endogenous to the at-risk population. Social vulnerability implies that groups and populations are vulnerable due to a lack of resources enabling them to respond and adapt to a hypothetical hazard. Therefore, studies dealing with social vulnerability rarely highlight one specific hazard. A third more novel approach examining vulnerability is to mix the physical and social approaches, incorporating aspects of both, foster phenomena-specific vulnerability indexes (Harlan, Brazel, Prashad, Stefanov, & Larsen, 2006; Johnson & Wilson, 2009; Johnson, Wilson, & Luber, 2009). As one might expect, incorporating data from multiple perspectives potentially represents a richer more robust solution to elucidating vulnerability than by relying on a singular physical environmental or social dataset.

One of the greatest gaps in the current understanding of vulnerability to extreme heat is its specific intra-urban nature. Place is perhaps the most vital component in vulnerability as it is ubiquitous in an examination of most phenomena. In order to assist in the understanding of extreme heat-health risk and to further catalyze the development of models highlighting such risk, the research presented in this article demonstrates the development of an extreme heat vulnerability index (EHVI). The EHVI incorporates an approach utilizing well-recognized variables, both physical and social, which are known to contribute to extreme heat vulnerability. This effort is dissimilar to previous studies that have either examined variables (both environmental and social) to determine which are most indicative of heat-related health risk, or have sought to create an encompassing index without relating it to heat-related mortality or health outcomes (Harlan et al., 2006; Reid et al., 2009; Rinner et al., 2010; Uejio et al., 2011). This research seeks to fill this void and intends to be recognized as an evolution of heat-related vulnerability modeling in the context of previous findings. Moreover, this is the first significant spatial analysis of the Chicago 1995 extreme heat event, which includes a significant number of decedents (*n* = 586) in which to approximate vulnerability.

## Background

Extreme heat, punctuated by heat waves or extreme heat events (EHE), is the primary cause of weather-related mortality in the United States (Luber & McGeehin, 2008; Wilhelmi & Hayden, 2010). Several communities have county wide heat warning systems, but determining variations in vulnerability within localized areas is a developing functionality that should significantly contribute to future mitigation plans of heat-related health concerns (Harlan et al., 2006; Kalkstein, 1991, Kalkstein & Greene, 1997; Kalkstein, Jamason, Greene, Libby, & Robinson, 1996; Wilhelmi & Hayden, 2010). Currently the most widely used method of spatially specific heat warnings is the Heat-Health Watch Warning System (HWWS), utilized by the National Weather Service (NWS) of the United State’s National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) (Kalkstein, 1991, Kalkstein et al., 1996). This system is currently employed by approximately 20 cities in the United States and focuses on atmospheric conditions which have previously contributed to heat-related mortality. The greatest limitation of this framework is the lack of spatial specificity when determining localized variations in risk, as it focuses on larger spatial entities such as city or county boundaries (Harlan et al., 2006; Johnson & Wilson, 2009; Johnson et al., 2009; Kalkstein, Greene, Mills, & Samenow, 2011; Smoyer, 1998; Smoyer-Tomic, Kuhn, & Hudson, 2003).

Numerous studies have attempted to address the lack of spatial specificity in heat warnings at the local level (Harlan et al., 2006; Johnson et al., 2009; Uejio et al., 2011; Wilhelmi & Hayden, 2010). These approaches are heavily influenced by advanced geospatial technologies such as remote sensing and geographic information systems. Utilizing these systems provides a robust modeling framework that places emphasis on the explicit spatial nature of natural hazards. Moreover, these techniques provide a foundation on which to fuse both social and environmental data sources in a way analogous to hybridization. Extreme heat, as with all natural hazards, is best understood by utilizing a social environmental approach due to the natural and latent complexities inherent in vulnerability (Huang et al., 2011; Miron, Montero, Criado-Alvarez, Diaz, & Linares, 2010; Pantavou, Theoharatos, Mavrakis, & Santamouris, 2011; Rinner et al., 2010; Wilhelmi & Hayden, 2010).

Thought to contribute to the health risks of extreme heat in urban settings, the urban heat island (UHI) is strongly related to the built environment (Dousset et al., 2011; Johnson & Wilson, 2009; Papanastasiou, Melas, Bartzanas, & Kittas, 2010; Stone, Hess, & Frumkin, 2010; Tan et al., 2010; Thorsson, Lindberg, Bjorklund, Holmer, & Rayner, 2011; Zhou & Shepherd, 2010). The UHI effect is generally described as the prevailing differences between the air and surface temperatures in the city contrasted to those temperatures in the adjacent rural hinterland. It is important to distinguish between two notably different types of UHI effect. The primary effect (historically observed first) is currently known as the canopy urban heat island (Lo & Quattrochi, 2003). This is the traditional view, where the entire urban area was though to exhibit a singular, and continuous, higher ambient air temperature than surrounding rural areas. The second type is the surface UHI that is observational through current satellite technologies registering thermal characteristics (land surface temperature, emissivity) (Wang, Zhu, & Wang, 2004; Weng, Lu, & Schubring, 2004). This is a measure of surface temperature and is not a direct metric of the sensible temperature of the environment. Important to note is that LST is not a measure of the air temperature but of the surface being imaged. The dichotomous interaction between the two (air temperature and LST) is an area of ongoing research within urban climatology. Strong evidence exists that there is a significantly positive relationship between the surface and ambient air temperature (Voogt & Oke, 2003; Weng & Quattrochi, 2006). However, intra-urban variations in temperature are much more apparent within the surface UHI due to the resolution of measurement with satellite remote sensing techniques and the spatial distribution of materials consistent with the built environment. These pockets of extremes in temperature within the UHI are termed micro-urban heat islands and are strongly related to the land cover present in the area of consideration (Aniello, Morgan, Busbey, & Newland, 1995; Dousset & Gourmelon, 2003; Smargiassi, Fournier, Griot, Baudouin, & Kosatsky, 2008). Considering this trait of the UHI effect, it is possible that certain areas of a city might experience episodes of extreme heat while other areas within the city, only a few hundred meters away, would not approach the same extreme heat threshold. Such a detailed local understanding could result in the delineation of smaller scale extreme heat alert procedures.

The social aspect of extreme heat-health risks is a complicated mix of socioeconomic and other demographic characteristics; not to mention individualized behaviors and adaptations (Basu, 2009; Curriero et al., 2002; Harlan et al., 2006; Johnson & Wilson, 2009; Uejio et al., 2011). The demographic disposition of individual neighborhoods within a city is readily observable through the U.S. Census Bureau’s decadal census; although limitations exist for within decade projections. Primary population-based at-risk factors include: advanced age, lower levels of educational attainment, presence of children under 5, household income, and race. These same variables are present in many social vulnerability indices and without argue constitute a societal concern irrespective of the phenomena that is considered a hazard.

Entertaining both the social and environmental aspects of the health risks correlated with extreme heat exposure warrants the consideration of developing a heat specific vulnerability index. Many sociologists are familiar with the “SoVI” or the social vulnerability index pioneered by Cutter et al. (Andrew & Rockwood, 2010; Cutter, Burton, & Emrich, 2010; Schmidtlein, Deutsch, Piegorsch, & Cutter, 2008; Tate, Cutter, & Berry, 2010; Wood, Burton, & Cutter, 2010). This approach utilizes numerous demographic variables, as well as proximal relationships to social assets, to determine the level of social vulnerability for each county in the conterminous United States. SoVI has also demonstrated to be stable at levels of aggregation finer than the county level (i.e. census tract) (Schmidtlein et al., 2008). As its name suggests SoVI is not specific to any particular natural phenomena but is a global measure of vulnerability generalized to a variety of natural or societal hazards. The purpose of the present research is to generate a heat specific vulnerability index that we call the extreme heat vulnerability index (EHVI). The development of this proposed index follows previous work utilizing both social and environmental aspects of health vulnerability to extreme heat. This study is not the first to suggest the development of an EHVI. Reid et al. (2009) demonstrates an earlier attempt to develop such an index, called the EVI. Their study examined a more regional level index and was not critically examined in relation to health outcome data. However, Reid’s study does suggest local-scale testing and validation of the index; our work follows in their path. It is important to note that our research is different from the previously mentioned EVI and SoVI, because the EHVI can be considered a local index and therefore applicable to the location for which it is created. Moreover, we are not utilizing the same variables used in the SoVI or the EVI as our intention is to use the most widely available variables related to extreme heat vulnerability. The creation of the EHVI for other areas of interest would utilize similar variables of vulnerability, but their interplay and latency factors are likely localized due to the aforementioned interactive complexities.

## Methods

In order to develop and test the EHVI we selected a historic analog event, which occurred in Chicago, Illinois during the summer of 1995. This particular event is one of the primary EHEs that brought extreme heat to the general public’s attention (Browning, Wallace, Feinberg, & Cagney, 2006; Duneier, 2006; Shen, Howe, Alo, & Moolenaar, 1998). This EHE occurred during a 5-day period in Chicago, Illinois during July of 1995 and the mortality count was approximately 720 individuals. The extreme temperature was caused by a moist tropical (mT) air mass bringing exceptionally high temperatures and dew points into the Midwest region of the United States. Air temperatures were over 100 °F and surface dew point temperatures exceeded 80 °F, which led to dangerously high heat indices.

Mortality data was collected from the Illinois State Vital Records Department in Springfield, Illinois. No electronic record of the specific location of death was available. Therefore, each death certificate was digitally scanned and the cause of death, age of decedent, and location of death was encoded into a database for analysis and geocoding procedures. Once residential heat deaths were determined (*n* = 586; all 720 deaths did not meet our criteria of a residential heat death) these decedent records were geocoded using the census street centerline file for Chicago from the 1990 census (98% = correctly geocoded). The death locations were primarily geocoded as a test dataset for the development and evaluation of the EHVI.

Twenty-five census variables were selected at the census block group level from the 1990 decadal census that are widely considered to be indicative of vulnerability to extreme heat and were standardized by unit area (see Table 1). Previous research has demonstrated that the most prevalent indicators of vulnerability include: age, economic level, race, level of education, and social isolation (Dolney & Sheridan, 2006; Johnson & Wilson, 2009; Johnson et al., 2009; O’Neill, Zanobetti, & Schwartz, 2005). Cutter et al. (2003) identified that some of the previously mentioned variables which have the strongest associations with vulnerability, are the age of the population and an individual’s economic situation.

Age can indicate how efficiently an individual’s body is able to adapt to inclement weather and maintain normal thermoregulatory processes. Age can also allude to the quantity of social interactions and pre-existing health conditions, both of which are documented as extremely important factors for surviving an EHE (Cutter et al., 2003; Johnson & Wilson, 2009; Naughton et al., 2002; Whitman et al., 1997). Whitman et al. (1997) estimated more than 70 percent of the heat-related deaths during the Chicago, IL 1995 heat wave occurred in the 65 years of age or older population, an observation supported by many other researchers (Changnon, Kunkel, & Reinke, 1996; Dolney & Sheridan, 2006; Ebi, Teisberg, Kalkstein, Robinson, & Weiher, 2003). This is because elderly individuals have some of the highest prevalence of chronic illness rates within a population (Robinson, 2001; Schwartz, 2005; Shen et al., 1998). Pre-existing conditions cause damage to important organs and increase the risk of heart attack or stroke during natural thermoregulation. In cases of decreased motor function due to illnesses, such as Parkinson’s Disease or underdeveloped mental functions, can make it difficult for individuals to accurately asses their risk, relocate to cooler environments, or acquire fluids (CDC, 2002, 2006). Semenza et al. (1996) documented an increased risk of 16 percent for patients who were confined to bed, and a mortality rate six times greater for those who required the services of an attendant during adverse weather conditions. These facts alone demonstrate why age is considered such a vulnerable variable. Age variables also suggest higher probability of social isolation and fixed finances.

Economic status can also demonstrate vulnerability levels. In a study conducted by McMichael et al. (2008), countries with a low or mid economic ranking were found to have the highest risk to high temperatures. Poverty, in particular, consistently shows up in vulnerability studies, and can describe: the amount of government aid needed, level of education, or prevalence of less financially secure jobs (Changnon et al., 1996; Johnson et al., 2009; McMichael et al., 2008; Naughton et al., 2002). Economic indicators can also allude to local environmental impacts, such as: age or condition of housing, amount of adjacent vegetation, and availability of cooling amenities such as air condition or local public parks and pools (Cutter et al., 2003). Older buildings located in low rent and low income residential neighborhoods are harder to keep at an appropriate temperature, seldom have air conditioning, and are typically located within hazardous UHI areas (Davis, 1997). Being in an adverse environment during an EHE can have a significant impact on an individual’s survivability.

For this study, three environmental variables were selected and processed from a Landsat 5 Thematic Mapper image from July 1st, 1995 and were added to the previously mentioned census variables. This image was collected at approximately 11:00 am local time, which is near the time of maximum solar irradiance. The image was not collected during the heat event, as cloud cover did not allow for an unobstructed view of the city, ∼10% cloud cover over our area of interest. The chosen image was acquired during the satellite’s previous sweep of the area. Since the image was collected during the same season and was captured roughly one week before the EHE, it is assumed the thermal properties of the city are proportional to what occurred during the heat wave, allowing for comparison of the surface UHI during the heat event. The image has a spatial resolution of 30 m in the visible, near infrared, and middle infrared wavelengths and 120 m in the thermal channel. LST was calculated using a procedure that corrected for emissivity of varying land cover types specific to the Landsat 5 TM satellite (Chander, Markham, & Helder, 2009). We also processed the image to create the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI), as outlined by Huete. NDVI (NIR − Red/NIR + Red) highlights photosynthetically active vegetation; so is a measure of vegetation abundance (Huete, Hua, Qi, Chehbouni, & Vanleeuwen, 1992). It has previously been demonstrated the higher the amount of photosynthetically active vegetation, the lower the environmental land surface temperature of the sampled census block group (Gallo et al., 1993).

The normalized difference built-up index (NDBI) was also calculated to measure the abundance of built environment within the census block group (Chen, Zhao, Li, & Yin, 2006; Li & Yu, 2008; Zhang, Odeh, & Han, 2009; Zhang, Zhong, Wang, & Cheng, 2009). NDBI (NIR − MidIR/NIR + MidIR) is a measure of the abundance of components indicative of the built environment (i.e. manmade materials, impervious surface, etc.). Impervious surfaces have been shown to be strongly related to LST and the detrimental health effects of the UHI (Hu & Weng, 2009; Imhoff, Zhang, Wolfe, & Bounoua, 2010; Weng & Lu, 2008; Xiao et al., 2007; Yuan & Bauer, 2007; Zhang, Odeh, & Han, 2009; Zhang, Zhong, Wang, & Cheng, 2009). Values for NDBI are non-integer providing a continuous measure of built environment where the higher values are representative of larger amounts of human modified environment.

In order to determine measurements of our variables within the environment in which people live, we utilized the USGS National Land Cover Dataset (NLCD) map to extract land cover/land use patterns to identify areas representative of residential land use. The NLCD dataset was created in 1993. Using this delineation we calculated the average value of LST, NDVI, and NDBI within these zones for each block group as well as our denominator for areal standardization of the census block group level demographic variables. Therefore, all the census demographic variables are based on residential density. We view this as an important step because it generates statistics for the locations in which people reside and is not a simple standardization by the area of the arbitrary census block group boundary. For example, there could be a relatively large area within a census block group that contains an industrial site generating a large amount of heat waste and contains a significant portion of built environment, while no residence is on this site. By removing this potential confounding environmental relationship within the block group, it is thought to provide a better picture of the environment within residential areas. Moreover, there may be areas within a relatively large block group where people are very densely packed into residential zones. Standardizing our density measure by the area of the block group would construct an erroneous metric for how densely populated the residential zone is.

Factor analysis using principal components was then performed on the twenty-eight variables (census and environmental combined) collected at the block group level; before conducting the PCA we normalized all the variables to *Z*-score values. We employed a varimax rotation, to assist with interpretability of the output, and calculated regression factor scores for each component. Factor scores that surpassed the Kaiser criteria (eigenvalues > 1) were retained to explain variance in the dataset. Variables found to exhibit complex structure were removed in order to further assist in the ability to attempt to label the individual components. All scores from the remaining 19 variables were then added together following procedures outlined by Cutter (for the SoVI) and Reid (for EVI) to generate the EHVI (Cutter et al., 2003, 2008, 2010; Reid et al., 2009).

To test the effectiveness of the EHVI we calculated an expected mortality rate based on the total number of individuals living within a block group and the overall rate of death in Chicago during the EHE. We then compared the expected rate with a model of population density, socioeconomics, remotely sensed data, and the EHVI and tested for statistical significance. The models were then stratified by the standardized score from the summed PCA factors utilizing the following scheme:
1.
Greater than 2*Z*, High-High Risk (H-H)
2.
Less than 2*Z*, greater than 1*Z*, Low High Risk (L-H)
3.
Less than 1*Z*, greater than 0*Z*, High Moderate Risk (H-M)
4.
Less than 0*Z*, greater than −1*Z*, Low Moderate Risk (L-M)
5.
Less than −1*Z*, greater than −2*Z*, High Low Risk (H-L)
6.
Less than −2*Z*, Low Low Risk (L-L)

The population in each of the zones was calculated in order to determine the expected number of deaths. We then compared the expected number to the actual number of deaths occurring in each zone. If the EHVI is indeed effective one would expect there to be a higher rate of death in the H-H category with a general tapering of risk to the L-L zone. If the trend of mortality does not follow this pattern within the examination then we assume it to be invalid.

## Results

Table 1 presents the variables used in the study as well as the principal component structure of the EHVI. Component one loads heavily on 12 of the 19 variables used in the analysis and explains 46.71% of the variance. Component two loads heavily on 3 of the 19 variables and explains 13.90% of the variance. Component three explains 11.82% of the variance and loads heavily with 2 of the 19 variables. Similarly, accounting for 6.98% of the variance, component 4 contains 2 of the 19 variables. In this principal components solution: total population, males under 5, females under 5, males head of household, poverty under 5, poverty 65 and up, and below poverty level all exhibit complex structure in the PCA loadings matrix and were iteratively removed from the analysis until we found a matrix we believed to exhibit little to no complex structure.

Three alternative models were tested against the proposed EHVI, consisting of socioeconomic or environmental variables (Table 2). The comparison between these models demonstrates some interesting results. Population density does not appear to be a strong indicator of heat-related death, where only two categories differed significantly from the expected. The same results occurred for the LST model. Socioeconomic factors alone followed the rate of expectation with the only difference being the H-L category. The EHVI follows the expected trend of significantly higher deaths in the zones of greatest risk. The only exception within the EHVI model is the L-M category, which one would expect as the line of risk crosses from higher to lower risk, although this does not appear to be the case with the other models.

## Discussion

### Comparison between models

Examining the model developed utilizing population density (all models are presented spatially in Fig. 1) we do not see a significant increase in death over expected in the areas of greater settlement density. Therefore, there is not an indication of more death occurring in higher density areas than in lower density locations. There is a higher than expected death rate in the H-M category and a lower than expected rate in the L-M class. The remaining categories do not significantly differ from the expectation. This would seem to indicate that total population density is not a statistically significant factor in heat-related death. This has further been corroborated in previous studies elucidating the Philadelphia 1998 event (Johnson et al., 2009).

![Figure 1](https://api.elsevier.com/content/object/eid/1-s2.0-S014362281200032X-gr1.jpg?httpAccept=%2A%2F%2A)

Demonstration of the spatial distributions of each of the aforementioned models.

The model utilizing only LST does not perform better than the model utilizing population density. As with the previous model there is a higher rate than expected in the H-M category and less than expected in the L-M section. Utilizing this variable alone, it does not appear that there are greater than expected deaths in residential locations that exhibit extremes in heat, than in those that are closer to the background temperature associated with vegetated surfaces. This further corroborates studies demonstrating the social structure of heat-related health issues.

The model containing only socioeconomic variables arguably under-performs both the population density model and the LST only model. The H-L category has significantly less death than expected, while the other categories are similar to expectation. This finding seems to indicate that utilizing the socioeconomic variables alone does not account for much of the variation in heat-related death. Given this finding, it seems logical to mix the variables from both socioeconomic and environmental (remotely sensed) datasets to develop a better model of extreme heat-health risk, as is presented in this article by the EHVI model.

The EHVI model does follow the expected trend of greater than expected death in the higher risk categories and lower than expected in the lower risk zones. This is witnessed by a greater than expected death rate in the H-H, L-H, and H-M categories. The death rate is equal to expectation in the L-M category and less than expected in the H-L and L-L zones. Based on these findings the EHVI does appear to be a viable model at determining heat-related mortality risk by fusing data from socioeconomic and environmental assets.

### Components of the EHVI

Since the EHVI utilizes a principal components solution, a discussion of the components in further detail is warranted. Table 1 demonstrates component 1 (46.71% of the variance) contains much of the information on age, income, and educational status. Some of these variables we anticipated loading in a negative fashion; particularly the variables associated with income. However, the association within the component is the same between many of the variables. For example, population 65 and over in group living is assigned the same relationship (not inverse) as median income. This perhaps is demonstrative that the distribution of those 65 and over in group living is not necessarily an indicator of lesser socioeconomic capacity as was assumed at the beginning of the study. The variables associated with this factor contain a mixture of indicators, so it is difficult to label this component by either the economic indicators or the age indicators; it appears to be both.

Component 2 contains persons age 25 and over with only a high school education, the Hispanic population, and other races (races not fitting into the census designated categories) accounting for 13.90% of the variance. Tagging this component is equally difficult, but would seem to indicate those of lower educational status, accented by less socioeconomic means are at an increased risk. However, we have not encountered the finding that those both without a high school education and those with only a high school education are at increased risk in the literature. Clearly, further efforts need to be made to educate this group because of increase weather-related risk.

Component three contains 2 of the 3 physical/environmental variables examined in the study. The NDVI and NDBI are both present in this component and together explain 11.82% of the variance. As one would expect, the relationship between the two is inverse; higher amounts of vegetation equal less built environment and lower amounts of vegetation equal greater amounts of built environment. The relationship between these two variables is easier to visualize as component 3 seems to be most indicative of the built environment and vegetation amounts. As noted earlier these variables are also strongly associated with the UHI effect, but are not direct measures of it as LST is.

Component 4 is again difficult to place into a named category. This component contains both the black population and LST variables. Although, the relationship between the surface UHI and the black population distribution has been observed before (Philadelphia, 1993 EHE) it remains confounding to explain appropriately. We did not explore the racial differences in heat-related death, within our mortality dataset, which might provide a more robust explanation of this relationship.

The environmental variable of LST and black population (component 4 and 5) associated with increased risk only accounted for 11.848% of the variance for the spectrum of vulnerability examined. We anticipated the environmental LST would account for more variance since previous studies have demonstrated very strong relationships between environmental variables (especially land surface temperature) and heat-related vulnerability (Dousset et al., 2011; Harlan et al., 2006; Johnson & Wilson, 2009; Johnson et al., 2009). However, if we include all measures we utilize for the UHI (LST, NDVI, NDBI) the EHVI accounts for 18.80% of the variance in vulnerability. Additional examinations need to be undertaken to link the relationship between land surface temperature and heat-related mortality as there are some apparent inconsistencies in the present literature. Uejio et al. found the “distribution of heat was inconsequential” for the 1998 heat wave in Philadelphia, using nighttime ASTER imagery. Hattis et al. recently found no relationship between heat-related death and their measure of urbanization in Massachusetts (Hattis, Ogneva-Himmelberger, & Ratick, 2012). Dousset found mortalities in France were strongly related to nighttime land surface temperature but not to daytime temperatures (Dousset et al., 2011). Further, Johnson et al., found that land surface temperatures were a strong predictor of mortality in Philadelphia during the 1993 EHE (Johnson & Wilson, 2009; Johnson et al., 2009). Further, the former study also showed a strong relationship between the distribution of the surface UHI and the spatial distribution of the black population. These results seem to corroborate that particular finding. However, previous inconsistencies in the aforementioned studies could be due to the complex nature of the phenomena of extreme heat and could further be a product of the different remote sensing instruments and methods utilized.

This study incorporates some limitations that warrant further discussion. In particular is the use of LST as the measure of temperature rather than the ambient air temperature recorded by an *in situ* instrument. Depending on meteorological conditions present during the acquisition of the satellite image the relationship between ambient air temperature and LST can be quite different. Moreover, daily (likely highly dispersed) cloud coverage during the heat event could contribute to cooling effects not accounted for by a “snapshot” from a remotely sensed instrument. These temporal limitations are often encountered in studies incorporating remotely sensed imagery. We felt for an intra-urban study that there was not a sufficient number of *in situ* instruments present in Chicago to accurately interpolate an ambient air temperature layer given the high spatial frequency of the urban landscape.

Additionally, there are other variables, specifically socioeconomic, that we have not included in our study. One in particular is the observed presence of an air conditioning unit in a home. We decided to not include this variable as it seemed likely correlated with economic status and it also assumed usage of the air conditioning system. Those with lower economic means might not utilize a present air conditioning system due to the cost associated with its operation.

## Conclusions

This study demonstrates a relatively straightforward method of determining vulnerability to extreme heat. The variables utilized have been incorporated in previous studies of extreme heat vulnerability. However, most previous studies sought to determine which socioeconomic or environmental variable was most similar to mortality or morbidity from extreme heat. This study incorporates socioeconomic measures of extreme heat vulnerability along with environmental indicators in a principal components analysis to initiate the development of an extreme heat vulnerability index (EHVI).

The socioeconomic variables accounted for most of the variance (∼70%) in vulnerability for Chicago during the 1995 heat event. The environmental variables (surface temperature, NDVI, NDBI) accounted for less variance than expected. However, they arguably accounted for a significant portion of the variance (∼12%) and warrant inclusion in the index. The EHVI accounted for nearly 80% of the variance associated with variables currently thought of as leading contributors to heat-related mortality. This research demonstrates a robust and significant model of vulnerability that is fairly easily employed but potentially computationally intensive. Further indications from this and previous studies suggest that extreme heat vulnerability is a complex local-scale phenomenon that should be examined cognizant of these traits.

The proposed technique could be further employed in other locations to examine the unique relationships between socioeconomic and environmental vulnerability. Therefore, we consider it an applied index that is primed for implementation and testing. Similar systems to examine air quality and its relationship to heat are being developed and applied in numerous locations (Merbitz, Buttstädt, Michael, Dott, & Schneider, 2012). These types of analyses are warranted simply for their potential to provide numerous applications to extreme heat, as well as other disaster, response plans for municipalities. Similar analysis could be used to support decision processes before a municipal heat wave or during the disaster itself to benefit mitigation. For example, similar analysis could be used to provide “intelligence-led” decisions for the placement or incorporation of emergency cooling centers – among other pertinent issues – into municipal heat response plans (Miles & Chang, 2011). Many cities and municipalities have a “heat plan” that would be initiated in an episode of extremely hot weather. However, most of these plans lack spatial awareness within the city and would benefit from cognizance of the spatial distribution of vulnerability, thereby making the plan and its implementation more effective. For example, a spatially-explicit map of vulnerability could aid emergency response by anticipating locations of greatest need during a heat wave, allowing for the placement of additional medical transportation (ambulances) or increased staffing of emergency departments to accommodate the increases in heat-related emergency visits. Longer time-horizon benefits could include enhancement of UHI mitigation plans by targeting urban cooling strategies (cool/green roof programs, urban canopy projects) within the most vulnerable neighborhoods. Models such as presented here could be utilized to determine the amount of urban tree canopy increase needed to effectively cool a specific neighborhood.

Making extreme heat even more complex is the fact that extreme temperatures in Chicago, IL would not necessarily prompt a health concern in Phoenix, AZ for the same meteorological conditions. Therefore, if an index were developed that demonstrated the different “levels” of vulnerability on a regional scale, they might be misconstrued and not pertinent to the local-scale phenomena of interest and provide a potentially skewed image of vulnerability. Therefore, we encourage the local-scale creation and analysis of vulnerability indices specific to individual cities or locations. Thereby, we lower the probability of ecological and atomistic fallacy, and focus attention on the local-scale interactions and perturbations. Utilizing the methods demonstrated in this study for another city, one should be able to develop a local model of extreme heat vulnerability and sufficiently test the output with health outcome data (morbidity, mortality, etc.), provided it is readily available.

Obviously, extreme heat is more than an academic concern to the public health and modeling community. It currently is the number one weather-related cause of mortality and its burden on health is likely underreported due to the difficulty in defining heat-related morbidity (Luber & McGeehin, 2008; Wilhelmi & Hayden, 2010). Incorporating analysis such as outlined in this research could lead to further developments in heat-related mitigation and alert systems. Future work should hinge on the intricate balance between socioeconomic and environmental vulnerability and potentially treat extreme heat and its associated vulnerability as a complex adaptive system. Cellular Automata (CA), has the unique ability to model complex intricate proximal interactions and could possibly be utilized to simulate extreme heat episodes utilizing the variables presented in this study. Further, Self Organizing Maps (SOM), have demonstrated the ability to outperform PCA at dimensionality reduction and explanation of variance. A study examining the creation of an EHVI utilizing this approach could provide some interesting results that would warrant SOM inclusion in a practical manner. As this and other previous studies have demonstrated, vulnerability to extreme heat is a complex mix of social and environmental interactions. Future work should further enhance our understanding and resiliency when approached by this complex, unique and increasing threat.
